Cipher-X Omega

Memory over Files

Cipher-X Omega compares repeated images of the same sky to find objects that moved, or that changed in brightness or spectrum. It is demonstrated here on five SPHEREx epochs of comet 3I/ATLAS from 14 December 2025, with Gaia DR3 and NEOSSat cross-checks.

Survey telescopes re-image the whole sky on a regular cycle, but the images are stored as large expert files (FITS). At survey scale no one can inspect them all, so change between visits is hard to find. This page states the data used, the method, the measured results, and the limits of the demonstration.

Cipher-X Crew — Pakistan and India. Team credits are listed at the end of this page.

Tested example

Method — two kinds of change

An object in a repeated survey can change in two ways: where it is, and what it measures. This tool checks both.

Change 1 · Position

Where it changed

Epochs are registered to one sky grid and compared by blinking or by subtraction. Fixed stars cancel out. An object that moved leaves a vacated position and an appeared position. This is measured in the blink comparator and the difference imaging below.

Change 2 · Spectral fingerprint

What it measures

Each object is also recorded as a set of flux measurements at the wavelengths sampled on each visit — its spectral fingerprint. If a later visit's measurements no longer match the earlier record, the object has changed in brightness or spectrum, whether or not it moved.

Why a moving object is sampled at new wavelengths

SPHEREx detectors carry a linear-variable filter: the wavelength sampled at a point depends on where on the detector the light lands. A moving object therefore lands at a different sampled wavelength in each frame. Comet 3I/ATLAS was sampled as follows across the five epochs (flux in MJy/sr·px, aperture photometry):

Fixed stars are sampled the same way, visit by visit, at the wavelengths corresponding to their detector positions. Their fingerprints are shown in the Fingerprint Lab.

Proposed idea

Fingerprint memory at survey scale

At survey scale, each object's measurements could be stored as one compact record — the comet's record above is under 1 KB, against about 6.4 MB for one FITS cutout — and a mismatch between visits (a Δ-fingerprint) would flag the object for inspection. This is demonstrated as a concept on the single field here; searching fingerprints across the full survey is future work (see Limits).

Existing tools

Existing public tools each cover part of this method: Backyard Worlds: Planet 9 and Backyard Worlds: Cool Neighbors use volunteers blinking WISE images to find movers; SPIFF (Gagné et al. 2026) extracts SPHEREx spectrophotometry of known moving sources; IRSA provides archive access and a moving-object search tool for known objects. This page combines epoch comparison and per-object spectral records in one viewer, applied to the dataset above.

Tested example

Look up a patch of sky

Enter the coordinates of a patch of sky — right ascension and declination. The lookup checks which SPHEREx observations cover that point, and where a series is loaded on this page it opens the blink sequence below, so moving objects stand out like a short video.

Decimal degrees (167.1309, +5.1732) or sexagesimal (11:08:31.4, +05:10:23.5) are both accepted.

Try:
STEP 1

Query the archive

The coordinates are checked against the IRSA SPHEREx observation table (pipeline step 13, 13_patch_finder.py): every level-2 image whose footprint contains the point is an epoch of that patch.

STEP 2

Build the series

Matching epochs are cut out at the same size, registered to one sky grid and given a shared stretch — the same preparation used for the five frames below.

STEP 3

Blink it

The series plays in time order in the blink comparator. Stars stay fixed; anything that moved jumps between frames.

This page is a static snapshot, so it ships with one patch fully loaded — the comet field, with its five December 2025 epochs ready to blink below. The archive query itself (step 13) runs for any coordinates from the project repository; serving freshly cut-out image series for arbitrary coordinates inside this page is the remaining hosting step, stated under Limits.

Tested example

Difference imaging: epoch 5 minus epoch 1

Two epochs are registered to the same grid and subtracted. Fixed stars cancel; an object that moved leaves a vacated/appeared pair. Clusters above 5σ are detected, then filtered for artifacts.

STEP 1

Register

Both epochs reprojected onto one shared sky grid, so fixed stars align.

STEP 2

Subtract

Epoch 5 minus epoch 1. The static sky cancels; only change remains.

STEP 3

Detect ≥ 5σ

Connected clusters above five times the noise: 158 candidate clusters in the raw difference.

STEP 4

Reject artifacts

Filter cosmic rays, star residuals and noise. What remains is the mover list.

Difference image, epoch 5 − epoch 1. Blue: present in epoch 1, absent in epoch 5 (vacated). Red: present in epoch 5, absent in epoch 1 (appeared). The comet is the pair at centre-left and far right, joined by its dotted track.

What the filter removes

Most of the 158 raw clusters are artifacts, in three classes: cosmic-ray spikes (single pixels, no extent — rejected by size); bright-star band residuals (a star's flux differs between the D2 and D3 bands, so it does not cancel — rejected because a Gaia star sits at that position); and noise clusters (rejected by the 5σ cut and minimum cluster size). A genuine mover is extended, appears as a vacated/appeared pair, and has no catalogued star at either position.

Outcome

After artifact rejection, the comet's pair is the strongest genuine mover in the field. The measured values, including a same-detector check (epoch 3 − epoch 1, both D2), are stated under Results.

Tested example

Motion fit and six-month projection

A least-squares straight-line fit to the comet's five measured positions gives its on-sky rate and the fit residuals (stated under Results). Extending that line six months forward gives the projected position below.

Projected position, +6 months

RA 325.54° · Dec +75.36°

Target date: 14 June 2026, the next SPHEREx all-sky pass.

This is a straight-line illustration of the projection, not an ephemeris. Real orbits are curved; over 182 days the comet's true position differs from this point (see Limits).

What the fit is used for

The fit converts five positions into a rate and a direction, which is what a follow-up observation needs: where to point, and when. The same fit supplied the comet's interpolated position inside the NEOSSat frame analysed below — that frame's time falls between epochs 3 and 4, so the position is an interpolation, not an extrapolation.

External check — JPL Horizons

The five measured positions were compared with NASA JPL's independent Horizons ephemeris for the comet (C/2025 N1, geocentric) at the same five times. The measured and ephemeris positions agree to 0.23″, 0.11″, 0.04″, 0.33″ and 0.07″ — within 0.33″ at every epoch, less than a tenth of a SPHEREx pixel (6.2″). A straight-line fit to the Horizons positions gives the same rate and direction: 1.1673° per day, PA 289.27°. The fit residuals alone only show the five points are consistent with each other; this check shows they are also correct against an independent orbit solution.

MeasurementValue
On-sky motion rate1.167° per day (175″ per hour), position angle 289.3°
Motion fit qualityResiduals 0.31″ RMS across the five epochs; total travel 1,431″ (0.40°) in 8 h 10 min
Independent validation — JPL HorizonsMeasured positions agree with the JPL Horizons ephemeris (C/2025 N1) to ≤ 0.33″ at all five epochs (0.23″, 0.11″, 0.04″, 0.33″, 0.07″). A fit to the Horizons positions gives the identical rate and direction: 1.1673°/day, PA 289.27°
Difference imagingAfter artifact rejection, the comet's vacated/appeared pair is the strongest genuine mover in the field. In the same-detector test (epoch 3 − epoch 1, both D2) the pair ranks 3rd and 4th among extended sources, peak SNR ≈ 294 and ≈ 253
Spectral samples (comet)Sampled wavelength 1.213 → 1.827 µm across the five epochs; measured flux 66.8 → 46.0

Limits

What this demonstration does not show, stated plainly.

  • Single wavelength slice per image. SPHEREx level-2 images are single-plane LVF images: one cutout records one wavelength slice per object, not a spectral cube. A full 102-band spectrum requires many visits per object.
  • Two detector bands are mixed. Epochs 1–3 are detector D2 and epochs 4–5 are detector D3, so flux steps between epoch 3 and epoch 4 combine the band change with any real change in the object.
  • The NEOSSat frame does not show the comet. In the single 15 s frame analysed, the comet is not detected; the control test (400 random positions) confirms the measurement is consistent with blank sky.
  • The +6-month position is not an ephemeris. It is a straight-line extension of the measured track, shown to illustrate the projection method. Real orbits are curved.
  • Demonstrated on a known object. The comet, its field and its approximate positions were known in advance. A blind run — the same pipeline on a field that has not been pre-solved — has not yet been demonstrated.
  • No recovery statistics yet. No injection test (planting a synthetic mover and checking the pipeline recovers it) has been run, so no false-positive or completeness rate is quoted. The result is one object in one field.
  • Coordinate lookup is pre-loaded for one patch. The patch finder (pipeline step 13) lists the SPHEREx epochs covering any RA/Dec, and runs from the project repository. This static page ships with cutouts loaded only for the comet field, so blinking an arbitrary patch inside the page still needs a small hosted service to cut out and serve that series on request.
  • No Planet X detection is claimed. The method is demonstrated on a comet. Applying it to slow-moving candidates would require survey-scale data across repeat surveys, which this single-field demonstration does not use.
  • Future work. A search backend (FastAPI + Qdrant) for fingerprint records at survey scale; assembly of full 102-band spectra per object; stacking of all 44 NEOSSat frames; automated ingestion of new SPHEREx releases.

Resources

The eight official challenge resources — four from NASA, four from the Canadian Space Agency — and what each was used for.

NASA · 1 of 8

IRSA SPHEREx Archive

Source of the five frames (Quick Release 2 level-2 images, via the IRSA cutout service), the difference imaging and all photometry.

NASA · 2 of 8

SPHEREx Tutorial Notebooks

Guided the processing approach: cutouts, WCS handling, and the per-pixel wavelength (WCS-WAVE) maps behind the fingerprints.

NASA · 3 of 8

WiseView

Blink comparison of aligned epochs — the basis of the comparator and the identification check.

NASA / ESA · 4 of 8

Gaia Mission Data

Gaia DR3: source of the field's star catalogue, the star labels, and the fixed-sky cross-match test.

CSA · 5 of 8

NEOSSat

Canada's asteroid-tracking microsatellite; its observations of this field on 13–14 Dec 2025 form the second-telescope section.

CSA · 6 of 8

CADC

The Canadian Astronomy Data Centre: its CAOM-2 service provided the NEOSSat cross-match, and its file service the retrieved science frame.

CSA · 7 of 8

NEOSSat Data Tutorial

Guided how NEOSSat observations are structured and queried.

CSA · 8 of 8

NEOSSat Dataset

The NEOSSAT collection: 773,583 observations, 4,417 targeting "3I", 44 overlapping this field — one of them retrieved in full and analysed.

Methods note: IRSA cutout service → astropy / reproject onto a common WCS grid → per-image background subtraction and shared stretch → aperture photometry (r = 3 px, local annulus background) → difference imaging with MAD-based noise estimate → Gaia DR3 cone search with proper-motion propagation → CADC CAOM-2 queries → NEOSSat science frame retrieved via CADC, with aperture photometry at the motion-fit-interpolated comet position and a 400-position random control test → measured positions validated against the JPL Horizons ephemeris for C/2025 N1 at the five epoch times → coordinate lookups query the IRSA SPHEREx observation table for level-2 footprints containing the requested point (patch finder, pipeline step 13).
